title: The camera with no film
hook: You invented the digital camera. Can you survive it?

profit.label: Profit
profit.hint: Money the film business makes today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How ready Kodak is for what comes next

intro.text: It's 1975 and you run Kodak, the biggest name in photography. You sell the film, the chemicals and the paper. Every holiday snap in America makes you money.

lab.text: In December 1975, a 25-year-old Kodak engineer named Steve Sasson finishes a strange machine: an 8-pound box that takes a 100 by 100 pixel, black-and-white picture in 23 seconds and saves it to a cassette tape. You need a TV to see it. There is no film anywhere.

d1.title: The camera with no film
d1.setup: It's slow, ugly and blurry. But if it ever gets good, nobody will need your film.
d1.question: What do you do with the digital camera?
d1.advisor: The film division is nervous. Whatever you pick, they'll be watching.

options.label: Lock it in the lab. Film pays the bills, and this isn't ready.
options.outcome: Kodak patents the camera, but the executives who see it are not convinced. Sasson later recalled them doubting that anyone would want to look at their pictures on a television. No digital camera goes on sale.
options.why: Protecting your best business feels safe. But a new technology that looks worse at first can still replace you, and every year you wait, someone else learns it first.
options.better: Give digital to a small, separate team that's allowed to compete with film, and fund it from film profits.
options.takeaway: In 1975 you protected film instead of learning digital. Big companies rarely lose to better products; they lose to products they dismissed.

options.label: Set up a small, separate digital team that's allowed to compete with film.
options.outcome: You give Sasson twenty engineers, a separate building and one rule: don't ask the film division for permission. Film keeps paying the bills while the team learns sensors, storage and screens.
options.why: You kept the cash machine running while buying time to learn the next one. A separate team can't be strangled by the business it's meant to replace.
options.takeaway: In 1975 you funded digital in a separate team. Protect the core, but give the future its own room to grow.

options.label: Launch it now and beat everyone to digital.
options.outcome: You rush a camera into stores. It's bulky, slow and needs a television to view anything. Almost nobody buys it, and the loss shows up in your next annual report.
options.why: Right idea, wrong year. In 1975 there were no home computers and no screens worth viewing photos on. Being first is useless if customers can't use what you sell.
options.better: Keep developing it in a separate team, and launch when screens and storage are ready.
options.takeaway: In 1975 you were right about digital but too early. Timing is part of the decision, not a detail.

text.text: August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a small magnetic disk instead of film. It is not digital yet, but it needs no film, and it is on the front pages with Sony's name on it. You can still fix this.

August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Retailers panic. Your digital team isn't surprised; they've been building something similar for six years.
August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Your early camera flopped, but the world just caught up with the idea.

d2.title: Sony's filmless camera

setup.text: The board is uneasy about your last call. A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.
A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.

d2.question: How do you respond to Sony?

advisor.text: Careful. One more bad call and the board starts asking questions about you.
Film still makes most of our money. But this time the world is watching.

options.label: Tell investors it's a toy. Film pictures are still far better.
options.outcome: The stock holds steady and the camera counters keep selling film. Inside Kodak, the message is clear: digital is not a career move. Your best engineers start taking calls from Japan.
options.why: Early versions of a disruptive product are always worse. Comparing today's quality hides the real question: how fast is it improving?
options.better: Accept that digital is coming and start shifting money and people toward it while film is still strong.
options.takeaway: In 1981 you judged digital by today's quality instead of its speed of improvement.

options.label: Commission a study: how many years until digital beats film?
options.outcome: Your market-intelligence chief, Vince Barabba, reports back: digital could replace film, but Kodak has roughly ten years to prepare. Kodak does little to prepare.
options.why: The study was right about the threat. The mistake was treating 'ten years' as permission to wait. A deadline is only useful if you start moving before it.
options.better: Use the ten-year window to move money and talent into digital now, not in year nine.
options.takeaway: In 1981 you saw the threat clearly but treated the time window as comfort instead of a deadline.

options.label: Start moving film profits into digital imaging, starting now.

outcome.text: You pull the 1975 prototype out of the cupboard and put its inventor in charge. It's six years late, but Kodak still has the money, the patents and the brand to catch up.
You announce that a growing share of film profits will fund digital imaging every year. Wall Street grumbles about lower margins. Your engineers stop job hunting.

options.why: You used the cash from the old business to pay for the new one while you still could. That's the move most incumbents make too late.
options.takeaway: In 1981 you used today's profits to pay for tomorrow's business, before you were forced to.

text.text: It's 2001. Your digital cameras are among the best sellers in America, and people are starting to put their photos online. Kodak has just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Digital cameras are finally taking off and Kodak is selling them, but film is still where the money is. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Kodak's new EasyShare digital cameras have made it number two in the US, but film still earns most of the money. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.

d3.title: The photo website
d3.setup: Millions of people will soon put their photos online. But Kodak still earns its money from prints, paper and chemicals.
d3.question: What is Ofoto for?

advisor.text: This is your last warning from the board. Get this one wrong and they'll find a new CEO.
Every photo that stays on a screen is a print we never sell. But maybe that's the point.

options.label: Use it to sell prints. People upload, then order copies from us.
options.outcome: Renamed Kodak Gallery, the site grows to over 60 million users. But free accounts must keep buying prints or risk losing their photos.
options.why: You built the website around your old revenue instead of what customers wanted to do. The customer's job had changed from printing memories to sharing them.
options.better: Make it a free place to share photos with friends, and earn from the audience instead of paper.
options.takeaway: In 2001 you built for your old revenue instead of the customer's new habit.

options.label: Make it a free place to share photos with friends. Earn from the network.
options.outcome: Uploads are free, albums are easy to share, and friends comment on each other's photos. Within a few years, Kodak owns the place where families keep their pictures, just as phones start getting cameras.
options.why: You followed the customer's new habit, sharing, even though it hurt print sales. Owning the audience is worth more than owning the paper.
options.takeaway: In 2001 you followed the customer's new habit instead of your old revenue.

options.label: Shut it down. Put everything into selling digital cameras.
options.outcome: Kodak cameras fly off the shelves and the brand looks modern again. But every competitor is selling cameras too, and prices fall every year.
options.why: Cameras were a real business, but a crowded one with thin margins. You gave up the part of digital that customers come back to every day.
options.better: Keep the website and make it about sharing. That's where people would spend their time.
options.takeaway: In 2001 you chose hardware sales over owning where people's photos live.

text.text: It's 2007. Film sales are collapsing across the industry, but your digital businesses are growing fast enough to carry the company. You have a strong hand. Don't waste it.
It's 2007. Film sales are collapsing. Your digital business is real but not yet big enough to replace what film used to earn. This is your last big decision.
It's 2007. Film sales are falling fast. This is your last chance to save the company.

d4.title: The last chance
d4.setup: You have patents, chemistry expertise, factories and a famous name. Film won't come back.
d4.question: Where do you bet the company's future?
d4.advisor: Whatever we pick, we can only afford to do it properly once.

options.label: Fight to be the number one digital camera maker.
options.outcome: You win shelf space, then lose money on every price cut. Within a few years, the phone in everyone's pocket takes good enough pictures, and the standalone camera market starts to shrink.
options.why: You chose a market where prices only go down and a bigger threat, the phone, was already arriving.
options.better: Use what Kodak is best at, chemistry and materials, to enter new growing markets.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you fought for a market that was about to be eaten by phones.

options.label: Bet on home inkjet printers with cheaper ink.
options.outcome: In February 2007 Kodak unveiled EasyShare all-in-one printers, claiming its ink could cut the cost of printing a photo by up to half. They went on sale in March. The printers never became the big new business Kodak needed.
options.why: Cheaper ink was a smart pitch for a shrinking habit. You bet on people printing photos at home just as they started keeping them on screens.
options.better: Use Kodak's chemistry and materials know-how to enter new growing markets, as Fujifilm did.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you bet on a shrinking habit, home printing, instead of a growing market.

options.label: Use your chemistry know-how to enter new markets, like healthcare and materials.
options.outcome: You cut costs hard in film, then point your chemists at medical imaging, specialty films and materials. It's painful and slow, but new businesses start replacing what film used to earn. Fujifilm made a similar move and is still thriving.
options.why: You asked what Kodak was really good at, chemistry and materials, instead of what it used to sell. Skills travel to new markets; products don't.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you redefined Kodak by what it was good at, not what it used to sell.

legend.title: Kodak, still on top
legend.text: By 2012, Kodak is a digital imaging and materials company. Film is a small, profitable corner of the business. Business schools teach your story as the incumbent that disrupted itself.

survivor.title: Smaller, but alive
survivor.text: Kodak shrinks a lot, but it never goes bankrupt. You fixed enough, late enough, to keep the lights on. With a few earlier calls, it could have led the digital age.

collapse.title: Bankrupt in 2012
collapse.text: On January 19, 2012, Kodak files for bankruptcy. That April, Facebook buys Instagram, a photo-sharing app with 13 employees, for one billion dollars. The company that invented the digital camera lost the digital age.

fired.title: The board fires you
fired.text: Three bad calls. The board loses faith and replaces you. Your successor inherits a company that's falling behind, and the clock is still ticking.

realHistory: Kodak built the first digital camera in 1975, but its leaders were not convinced. It studied digital slowly after Sony's 1981 Mavica, used Ofoto to sell prints, and bet on home inkjet printers in 2007. It filed for bankruptcy on January 19, 2012 and emerged in 2013 as a much smaller company. Fujifilm, facing the same collapse, moved into healthcare, cosmetics and materials, and survived.
